home.title: Building a Mini 4WD starts here
home.intro: Mini 4WD Beginner's Guide is an unofficial fan site that catalogs Tamiya Mini 4WD kits, chassis and Grade-Up Parts. The builder above starts from the kit on your desk or from a bare chassis, lets you swap in upgrades one slot at a time, and checks the whole car against the race rules as you go.

steps.title: Three steps
steps.pick: Choose a kit or chassis: search by kit name or item number, or start from a bare chassis.
steps.swap: Swap parts slot by slot: tap a row in the list, or the part on the 3D car, to choose rollers, motors, gears and more. The picker lists only the parts that fit your chassis.
steps.check: Check and share: pick Open, Stock Class / B-MAX or Junior, see which parts break the rules, then send the build to a friend as a link.

chassis.title: Start from a chassis
chassis.intro: The chassis decides where the motor sits, whether it takes a single- or double-shaft motor, and which parts fit. Each chassis page lists its specs, stock parts and the kits built on it.

parts.title: Parts beginners change first
parts.intro: Most first upgrades are rollers, a motor and gears, and several chassis have a starter upgrade set of their own.

classes.q: What is the difference between Open and Stock Class / B-MAX?
classes.a: Open is Tamiya's official race regulation: use Tamiya parts, stay inside the size limits, and most modifications are allowed. Stock Class is Tamiya's entry-level class, run since 2025. It keeps the Open rules and adds more: no cutting the chassis, no new screw holes and no modifying the parts themselves. B-MAX GP unified its modification rules with Stock Class in December 2025. Before a race, check the rules the organiser publishes.

motors.q: What is the difference between single-shaft and double-shaft motors?
motors.a: A double-shaft motor has a shaft at each end and sits in the middle of the chassis, driving the front and rear wheels at once. The PRO chassis (MA, MS and ME) take one. Every other chassis takes a single-shaft motor at the front or the rear. The two do not swap, so know your chassis before you buy a motor. The builder only lists the kind that fits.

limits.q: What size and weight does a race car have to be?
limits.a: Tamiya's rules allow a car at most 105 mm wide, 165 mm long and 70 mm tall, weighing at least 90 g with batteries and motor, on tires 22 to 35 mm in diameter, running on two AA batteries. The builder cannot measure size or weight yet, so it lists those two rules as not checked.

categoryIntro.roller: Rollers sit at the front, rear and sides of the car and roll along the track wall to steer it through corners. Larger diameters corner more steadily; smaller ones are lighter with less drag, and rollers with built-in ball bearings spin more freely. The whole car, rollers included, must stay within 105 mm wide.
categoryIntro.plate: Reinforcing plates, in FRP or carbon, bolt to the front and rear of the chassis. They carry extra rollers, stiffen the car, and are the base most other upgrades mount on. Carbon is stiffer and lighter than FRP, and costs more.
categoryIntro.wheel-tire-set: A wheel and tire sold as a matched set. Small diameters accelerate faster and sit lower; large diameters reach a higher top speed. Regulations allow tire diameters from 22 to 35 mm.
categoryIntro.motor: The motor powers the car. Each model trades off speed, torque and battery draw, favouring acceleration or top speed. PRO chassis (MA, MS, ME) take double-shaft motors and all others single-shaft. Some motors are not allowed in Junior and other classes, so check class legality before buying.
categoryIntro.accessory: Things for the hobby rather than the car itself: double-sided tape, parts and motor cases, track pieces and display boxes.
categoryIntro.screw: Screws, nuts and washers that hold plates, rollers and other upgrades in place. Pick the length and head shape for where it goes; stainless steel screws are stronger than standard ones.
categoryIntro.gear: Gears carry the motor's turn to the axles. A higher ratio (such as 5:1) accelerates harder; a lower one (such as 3.5:1) reaches a higher top speed. Which gear sets fit depends on the chassis.
categoryIntro.body: Replacement body sets, clear bodies included. The body shell sets the car's look and affects its weight and centre of gravity; a lighter shell saves weight but is usually less durable.
categoryIntro.tire: Tires sold on their own. Soft tires grip better but add drag; hard tires roll faster but grip less in corners and on landings. Tire diameter must be between 22 and 35 mm.
categoryIntro.mass-damper: Metal weights mounted so they can move freely, soaking up the shock of landings and impacts so the car bounces and flips less. Where and how many you fit changes landing stability, at the cost of added weight.
categoryIntro.bearing: Bearings replace plastic bushings on the axles or gears, so parts spin more freely with less friction. They are one of the most common first upgrades for speed.
categoryIntro.stabilizer: Stabilizer heads and poles sit at the sides or underside of the car. When it touches the wall or edge of the track, they help it stay level instead of riding up or catching.
categoryIntro.spacer: Spacers, bushings, stoppers and hex mounts that set the heights and gaps between parts, such as roller height or axle play.
categoryIntro.chassis-set: Replacement chassis and chassis units, such as reinforced or lightweight chassis and front and rear units. Use them to change colour or material, or to replace a damaged chassis.
categoryIntro.brake: Brakes sit under the car and touch the track on slopes and jumps to scrub off speed, so the car does not fly off the course. The thickness and hardness of the brake sponge set how strongly it slows the car.
categoryIntro.wheel: Wheels sold without tires. Diameter, material and design change their weight and how quickly the car picks up speed; aluminium wheels need their own bushings.
categoryIntro.shaft: Axles join a pair of wheels and come in lengths such as 60 mm and 72 mm to suit the chassis. Reinforced and stainless steel shafts resist bending; hollow shafts are lighter.
categoryIntro.propeller-shaft: On single-shaft chassis, the propeller shaft carries drive from the motor to the axle at the other end, so all four wheels are driven. Each fits only the chassis whose length it is cut to; PRO chassis do not use one.
categoryIntro.terminal: The metal contacts between the batteries and the motor. Gold-plated terminals conduct better and resist corrosion, so less power is lost. Each set fits a particular chassis.
categoryIntro.bundle: Upgrade bundles for beginners, such as the per-chassis Basic Tune-Up Parts Sets, which put a few common upgrades in one box. A good first step if you have never modified a car.
categoryIntro.bumper: Front and rear bumpers and bumper units that protect the chassis from impacts and give rollers and plates somewhere to mount. Bumperless units save weight.
categoryIntro.body-catch: Catches that hold the body shell on the chassis. Quick-release and rubber catches make the body faster to take off and put back, for example when changing batteries.
categoryIntro.slide-damper: Roller mounts that slide sideways on springs. When a roller hits the wall, the mount gives and springs back, absorbing the shock so the car takes corners smoothly instead of bouncing off.
categoryIntro.gear-cover: Covers that keep dust and debris out of the gears and hold them in position. Reinforced versions last longer.
categoryIntro.sticker: Decorative stickers, and tapes that protect the body or chassis surface and reduce friction.
categoryIntro.other: Parts that fit no other category, such as rubber tubing, a motor cooling shield and motor brush holders.
categoryIntro.tool: Tools for maintaining and checking the car, such as a pinion puller and a speed checker.
categoryIntro.setting-tool: Tools for setting up the car, such as a checker box for the regulation length and width, and a flat setting board.
categoryIntro.motor-mount: A support that holds the motor in place so it does not shift or vibrate while running, keeping the drive steady.
